body.text: China’s transnational repression (often referred to as TNR) has attracted increasing international attention in recent years, particularly following revelations about Chinese overseas police stations operating all the way from Viña del Mar, Chile, to Rome, Italy. These cases have exposed how the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) attempts to extend its control beyond national borders, targeting dissidents, ethnic minorities, and political critics abroad. A similar pattern appears in Amnesty International’s 2024 investigation, which found that Chinese and Hong Kong students studying abroad self-censored for fear of the consequences of expressing themselves. However, while direct intimidation and surveillance have received considerable attention, subtler forms of repression remain largely overlooked.

Japan presents a particularly interesting case. Despite its geographical proximity to China, extensive economic relations, and large Chinese diaspora, the country has received comparatively little attention regarding the less visible forms of transnational repression. Japan’s democratic institutions and society reinforce the public assumption that individuals can safely express their political views, protected by academic freedom, the constitution, strong freedom of speech, and formal protection mechanisms. Only a few institutions, such as Human Rights Watch, have raised concerns over the issue.

Our recently published report, “Mapping CCP Transnational Repression in Japan: From Self-Censorship to Institutional Pressure,” goes further in challenging these assumptions about the absence of TNR in Japan. Based on 14 interviews conducted between July and November 2024 with academics, journalists, students, and activists, we identified three main mechanisms through which repression from Chinese individuals and institutions is experienced by critics in Japan: direct intimidation, institutional pressure, and self-censorship. The findings suggest that TNR does not require direct intervention. It can operate through existing social relationships, institutional incentives, and the fear of possible consequences.

The most recognizable form of transnational repression involves surveillance, harassment, and threats against individuals who criticize the CCP. Our interviews revealed several accounts consistent with these practices, affecting not only Chinese nationals but also Japanese academics and journalists.

For example, a Japanese journalist investigating Chinese overseas activities reported receiving eight anonymous phone calls in a single day. One featured an automated message instructing her to visit the Chinese embassy. Although the origin of these calls could not be independently verified – and calls purporting to be from the Chinese embassy are often scams rather than intimidation – their frequency and content raised concerns about her personal security.

Surveillance was another recurring concern. Activists described unidentified individuals photographing demonstrations, monitoring public events, and allegedly following participants afterward. During a Hong Kong-related event at a Japanese national university, we directly observed an attendee photographing activists and presentation materials before forwarding images through WeChat.

Several academics interviewed for our study described professional consequences associated with researching politically sensitive Chinese affairs. These included difficulty organizing events, colleagues’ reluctance to participate in research projects, and perceived obstacles to career advancement. One Chinese student even reported being advised to abandon a research topic because of its potential implications for China-Japan relations.

Another professor described colleagues declining to collaborate on sensitive research because they feared losing access to China. These experiences point toward a mechanism that is particularly difficult to identify: institutional complicity without necessarily requiring direct coordination with Beijing.

In such circumstances, organizations may restrict academic activities not because Chinese authorities explicitly demand it, but because they anticipate potential diplomatic, professional, or economic consequences.

Our interviews also raised concerns about some Chinese student associations in Japan. Several participants described associations allegedly facilitating information gathering and monitoring through student networks and WeChat groups. After hearing these testimonies, we found institutional connections linking Chinese institutions with the structure of several Chinese student associations, which are publicly available on official PRC-related websites. However, many of these institutions have been quite dormant in recent years.

Of course, the existence of official support and coordination from the Chinese embassy in Tokyo does not immediately mean that these institutions are used for repression, but the combination of testimonies, photographic evidence, and public information paint a picture that must be assessed as potential TNR.

One of the most significant findings concerns individuals who had never experienced direct intimidation but nevertheless restricted their own behavior. Three Chinese students interviewed for our research described avoiding politically sensitive classroom discussions and exercising caution when interacting with fellow Chinese nationals.

One student, despite having lived in Japan for five years, explained that he avoided political conversations even with close acquaintances. Another reported withholding opinions until others had expressed their positions.

These behaviors suggest that the consequences of authoritarian repression can persist beyond the authoritarian state’s territorial jurisdiction. More importantly, self-censorship can become normalized. Individuals who anticipate surveillance or retaliation may voluntarily restrict their expression without receiving explicit instructions.

Other interviewees described more direct pressure involving family members in China. One Chinese student reported receiving a call from police officers in his hometown shortly after arriving in Japan. The conversation ended with a warning to “be careful,” which he interpreted as an implicit threat. Such pressure is not unique to our interviewees. Human Rights Watch has documented similar cases in Japan, in which Chinese authorities contacted relatives back home to discourage political activism abroad.
This presents a particular challenge for democratic societies because the absence of visible coercion does not necessarily mean that freedom of expression is being fully exercised.

Japan’s response should combine institutional safeguards with a careful distinction between legitimate Chinese communities and activities intended to suppress political expression. Universities should establish transparent procedures for reporting intimidation, protecting sensitive student information, and ensuring that international partnerships do not compromise academic independence.

Policymakers should avoid treating Chinese students or diaspora organizations as inherently threatening. Such an approach risks reinforcing the mistrust and isolation that already discourage open discussion.

China’s TNR in Japan illustrates a challenge for liberal democracies. The greatest danger does not lie with the voices that were silenced, but in the culture of self-censorship that grows deep within a “democracy-protecting” society.
